children.label: a
children.prompt: Express $\sqrt3\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x$ in the form $R\sin(x-\alpha)$.

answer.worked:
Expand the sine difference and equate coefficients:
$$\begin{align*}\sqrt3\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x&=R(\sin x\cos\alpha-\cos x\sin\alpha)\\R\cos\alpha&=\sqrt3\\R\sin\alpha&=\sqrt3\\R&=\sqrt{(\sqrt3)^2+(\sqrt3)^2}=\sqrt6\\\tan\alpha&=\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt3}=1\end{align*}$$
Both $\cos\alpha$ and $\sin\alpha$ are positive, so choose $\alpha$ in the first quadrant.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=\frac\pi4\\\sqrt3\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x&=\sqrt6\sin\left(x-\frac\pi4\right)\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$y=\sqrt6\sin\left(x-\frac\pi4\right)$.

Amplitude $\sqrt6$; translate $y=\sin x$ right by $\frac\pi4$. The graph is shown below.
answer.worked:
From part a,
$$y=\sqrt6\sin\left(x-\frac\pi4\right).$$
Dilate $y=\sin x$ vertically by a factor of $\sqrt6$ and translate it right by $\frac\pi4$. The period remains $2\pi$.
The endpoints are $(0,-\sqrt3)$ and $(2\pi,-\sqrt3)$. The zeros are at $x=\frac\pi4,\frac{5\pi}4$, the maximum is $\left(\frac{3\pi}4,\sqrt6\right)$, and the minimum is $\left(\frac{7\pi}4,-\sqrt6\right)$.
